title: Guilty of loving
takeaway: If the world was made out of love, how can loving be a crime?
scene: The poet looks back at his youth. He trusted someone's promises, and it cost him. Now he asks how loving someone could ever be the wrong thing to do.

original: کسے دے قول تے اعتبار کر کے
میں بیٹھا ہاں جوانی خوار کر کے
transliteration: Kise de qaul te aitbaar kar ke
Main baitha haan jawaani khwaar kar ke
translation: I've ended up wasting my youth.
couplets.story: He believed someone's promises, and now he's sitting here having thrown away his best years.

original: ویلا بیتیا انج تکرار کر کے
transliteration: Vela beetiya inj takraar kar ke
translation: that's how the time went by, back and forth.
couplets.story: He kept begging, and the beloved kept saying no. Years passed like that, in one long argument.

original: کوئی ویکھے بھلا انکار کر کے
transliteration: Koi vekhe bhala inkaar kar ke
translation: My being is the one the angels bowed to;
couplets.story: Then he suddenly stands up for himself. He reminds everyone that God made human beings so honoured that He told the angels to bow to Adam. Nobody has the right to treat him as worthless.

original: اوہ پتھر دل کدے نہ موم ہویا
میں منتاں ویکھیاں سو وار کر کے
transliteration: Oh patthar dil kade na mom hoya
Main mintaan vekhiyaan sau vaar kar ke
translation: That heart of stone never once softened into wax,
though I tried pleading a hundred times.
couplets.story: He asked a hundred times. The beloved's heart stayed hard as stone. It never melted, not even a little.

original: عشق دے وہن وچ بیڑا عقل والا
میں شوہ چ ڈوبیا وچکار کر کے
transliteration: Ishq de vehn vich beera aql vaala
Main shauh ch dobiya vichkaar kar ke
translation: In the current of love, I took the boat of reason
out to the middle of the deep water and sank it.
couplets.story: Love is like a strong river. He was sailing on the 'boat' of common sense, and he deliberately sank it in the middle. Once you really love, being sensible goes overboard.

original: میں راکھی کرن لئی اپنی انا دی
دوالے بہہ گیا دیوار کر کے
transliteration: Main raakhi karan layi apni ana di
Dawaale beh gaya deewaar kar ke
translation: I built a wall all around me and sat inside it.
couplets.story: He admits his own mistake. To protect his pride, he walled himself in, and ended up alone behind it.

original: جے دنیا پیار دی تخلیق ہے اے
میں مجرم بن گیا کیوں پیار کر کے
transliteration: Je duniya pyaar di takhleeq hai ae
Main mujrim ban gaya kyon pyaar kar ke
translation: If this world was created out of love,
why have I become a criminal for loving?
couplets.story: This is the big question of the poem. If the whole world was created out of love, how can loving make him guilty of anything?

original: گیا کوئی کوٹھا مسمار کر کے
transliteration: Gaya koi kotha mismaar kar ke
translation: the house built from my affection, love and longing.
couplets.story: Everything he felt, his affection, his love, his hopes, was like a house he had built. Someone came along and knocked it flat.

original: میں احمدؔ اج وی پتن چیر سکناں
توں آوناں نئیں چھناں نوں پار کر کے
transliteration: Main Ahmad ajj vi pattan cheer saknaan
Toon aauna nahin Chhanaan nu paar kar ke
translation: Ahmad, even today I could cut straight across the ferry crossing,
but you won't come to me across the Chenab.
couplets.story: He ends with Punjab's old river love story. Like Sohni, who swam across the Chenab every night to meet her lover, he would still cross any river today. The sad part is that the beloved won't make that crossing for him.

deeper:
Two couplets carry this poem's spiritual weight. 'My being is the one the angels bowed to' recalls the Qur'an's story of Adam. Every human being carries a dignity given by God, so no rejection can make a person worthless.

'If this world was created out of love' echoes a saying Sufis love, in which God says: 'I was a hidden treasure, and I loved to be known, so I created the world.' If love is the reason anything exists, then loving cannot be a crime. Sinking 'the boat of reason' in the river of love is the Sufi idea that the heart reaches God where the calculating mind cannot.

Two other couplets are about the self. He sinks 'the boat of reason' in love's river, and he admits he built a wall around himself to guard his pride. Sufis teach that both have to go: the cold calculation and the walled-in ego.
why: It moves from a simple heartbreak to a big question: what is the world made of, and where do humans stand in it?
prompt: Have you ever had to choose between being 'sensible' and following your heart? What happened?
notes: The poem is printed in two columns: each row is one couplet, right-hand line first.
Last couplet, line 1: printed 'پٹ چیر' and read as 'pattan cheer' (cut across the ferry crossing). Needs a native check.
